Chapter 2 pretest: transformations and expectations

One block (about 25–30 min). No reading first. It decides which Chapter 2 sections need a lesson and which you skip.

How this works

Chapter 1 is finished: the check came back 15 of 15, and the proof was right. Next is Casella & Berger, Chapter 2, which has four sections you'll use for the rest of the book. For each one you get three questions: a concept, a calculation and a short proof, the same format as the Chapter 1 pretest.

  • "I don't know" is the honest answer, not a failure. It just means that section gets taught. A lucky guess skips a lesson you needed; if you guess anyway, say so with the "I guessed" button.
  • Proofs: 3–6 lines of plain text is fine ("integral from 0 to 1", "f_X", "g^-1"). I'm checking the idea and that each step is justified, not the typesetting.
  • Math boxes take expressions: type * for ×, /, ^ for powers, sqrt( ), exp( ). E.g. 3/5 - (3/4)^2.

Afterwards there is always a one-lesson summary of the whole chapter and a chapter check, plus lessons only for the sections you didn't know.

§2.1 Distributions of functions of a random variable

\(X\) has a continuous pdf \(f_X\), and \(Y = g(X)\) where \(g\) is decreasing with a differentiable inverse. Which is the pdf of \(Y\) on its support?

C&B Theorem 2.1.5. For decreasing \(g\), \(F_Y(y) = 1 - F_X(g^{-1}(y))\), and differentiating gives \(-f_X(g^{-1}(y))\,\tfrac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\), which is positive because the derivative of \(g^{-1}\) is negative. The absolute value writes the increasing and decreasing cases as one formula.

Adapted from Casella & Berger, Exercise 2.1(b), numbers changed. \(X\) has pdf \(f_X(x) = 5e^{-5x}\) for \(x > 0\), and \(Y = 2X + 3\). What is the value of the pdf of \(Y\) at \(y = 4\)? (An expression is fine, e.g. with exp( ).)

\(g^{-1}(y) = (y - 3)/2\) with derivative \(1/2\), so \(f_Y(y) = \tfrac{5}{2} e^{-5(y-3)/2}\) for \(y > 3\). At \(y = 4\): \(\tfrac{5}{2}e^{-5/2}\).

The probability integral transform (C&B Theorem 2.1.10), simplified. \(X\) has a continuous cdf \(F_X\) that is strictly increasing, and \(Y = F_X(X)\). Prove that \(P(Y \le y) = y\) for \(0 < y < 1\), so \(Y\) is uniform on (0, 1).

For 0 < y < 1: P(Y ≤ y) = P(F_X(X) ≤ y) = P(X ≤ F_X^{-1}(y)) (F_X strictly increasing, so it has an inverse and applying it keeps the inequality) = F_X(F_X^{-1}(y)) (definition of the cdf) = y (continuity: F_X takes every value in (0, 1)). Full marks: the step that applies the inverse is justified by "strictly increasing". Partial: the chain is right but no justification for inverting.

\(P(Y \le y) = P(F_X(X) \le y) = P(X \le F_X^{-1}(y)) = F_X(F_X^{-1}(y)) = y\). Inverting is allowed because \(F_X\) is strictly increasing; continuity makes \(F_X^{-1}(y)\) exist for every \(y\) in (0, 1). The book's version handles flat stretches of \(F_X\) with \(F_X^{-1}(y) = \inf\{x : F_X(x) \ge y\}\).

§2.2 Expected values

\(X\) has pdf \(f_X\) and \(g\) is a function. To compute \(E\,g(X)\), you…

\(E\,g(X) = \int g(x) f_X(x)\,dx\) over the support of \(X\) (C&B Definition 2.2.1; the "two-way rule", equation 2.2.5, says it agrees with \(E\,Y\) for \(Y = g(X)\)). You don't need the distribution of \(g(X)\). Applying \(g\) to \(E X\) works for linear \(g\), not in general.

\(X\) has pdf \(f_X(x) = 3x^2\) for \(0 < x < 1\). What is \(\operatorname{Var} X\)? (A fraction or an expression.)

\(E X = \int_0^1 3x^3\,dx = 3/4\) and \(E X^2 = \int_0^1 3x^4\,dx = 3/5\), so \(\operatorname{Var} X = 3/5 - 9/16 = 3/80\).

C&B Example 2.2.6. Assume \(E X^2 < \infty\). Show that \(E(X - b)^2\) is minimized over constants \(b\) at \(b = E X\).

Write E(X − b)² = E(X − EX + EX − b)² and expand: E(X − EX)² + 2(EX − b)E(X − EX) + (EX − b)²; the middle term is 0 because E(X − EX) = 0 (linearity, Theorem 2.2.5); so E(X − b)² = Var X + (EX − b)², smallest when b = EX. Calculus is also fine: differentiate in b, set 2b − 2EX = 0, check the second derivative is positive. Full marks: why the cross term vanishes (or the second-derivative check).

\(E(X - b)^2 = E\big((X - EX) + (EX - b)\big)^2 = E(X - EX)^2 + (EX - b)^2\), because the cross term is \(2(EX - b)E(X - EX) = 0\). The first term doesn't depend on \(b\), and the second is 0 exactly when \(b = EX\).

§2.3 Moments and moment generating functions

Two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) have the same moments of every order, \(E X^r = E Y^r\) for \(r = 1, 2, \dots\). Must they have the same distribution?

C&B Theorem 2.3.11 and Example 2.3.10: two different distributions (one is the lognormal) share every moment. Equal moments settle it when both supports are bounded, or when the mgfs exist and agree on a neighbourhood of 0.

\(X\) has moment generating function \(M_X(t) = \dfrac{3}{3 - t}\) for \(t < 3\). What is \(E X^2\)?

\(E X^2 = M_X''(0)\) (Theorem 2.3.7). \(M_X'(t) = 3/(3-t)^2\), \(M_X''(t) = 6/(3-t)^3\), so \(M_X''(0) = 6/27 = 2/9\). (This is the exponential distribution with mean 1/3.)

C&B Theorem 2.3.15. \(X\) has mgf \(M_X(t)\), and \(a, b\) are constants. Show that the mgf of \(aX + b\) is \(e^{bt} M_X(at)\).

M_{aX+b}(t) = E e^{t(aX+b)} (definition of the mgf) = E(e^{bt} e^{(at)X}) = e^{bt} E e^{(at)X} (e^{bt} is a constant; linearity) = e^{bt} M_X(at) (definition again, evaluated at at). Full marks: the definition used at both ends and the constant pulled out with a reason.

\(M_{aX+b}(t) = E\,e^{t(aX+b)} = e^{bt}\,E\,e^{(at)X} = e^{bt} M_X(at)\): the factor \(e^{bt}\) is a constant, so it comes out of the expectation.

§2.4 Differentiating under an integral sign

For differentiable \(f(x, \theta)\), \(a(\theta)\), \(b(\theta)\), Leibnitz's rule gives \(\dfrac{d}{d\theta}\displaystyle\int_{a(\theta)}^{b(\theta)} f(x, \theta)\,dx\) as…

C&B Theorem 2.4.1: one term for each moving limit (the fundamental theorem of calculus plus the chain rule, with a minus sign at the lower limit) and the integral of the partial derivative for the integrand's own dependence on \(\theta\).

Let \(I(\theta) = \displaystyle\int_0^{\theta} \theta x^2\,dx\). What is \(I'(\theta)\) at \(\theta = 2\)?

Leibnitz: \(\theta \cdot \theta^2 \cdot 1 + \int_0^\theta x^2\,dx = \theta^3 + \theta^3/3 = 4\theta^3/3\), which is \(32/3\) at \(\theta = 2\). Check: \(I(\theta) = \theta^4/3\) directly.

Over an infinite range you can't always swap \(\tfrac{d}{d\theta}\) and \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\). State a condition that makes the swap legal, and say in a sentence or two what it rules out.

Any correct sufficient condition: there is an integrable function g(x) with |∂f(x, θ)/∂θ| ≤ g(x) for all x and all θ near θ₀ (a dominating function; C&B Corollary 2.4.4), or the book's Theorem 2.4.3 version with difference quotients bounded by g(x, θ₀) and ∫ g < ∞. What it rules out: the derivative's mass escaping to infinity (the derivative growing in x in a way no single integrable function controls), so the limit of the difference quotients can't be moved inside the integral. Full marks: a dominating integrable bound, uniform in θ near θ₀. Partial: "f is differentiable" or "the integral converges" alone.

The usual condition: an integrable \(g(x)\) with \(\left\lvert \tfrac{\partial}{\partial\theta} f(x, \theta)\right\rvert \le g(x)\) for every \(x\) and every \(\theta\) near \(\theta_0\). Then dominated convergence moves the limit of difference quotients inside the integral. Without it, mass can escape to infinity and the two sides differ.
